transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-09-09 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Lena Park (Redwood AE), Diego Marquez (Redwood SE), Rachel Chen (Redwood Security PM); Asha Gupta (CISO, Pioneer), Tom Reynolds (Head of Platform), Dr. Mei Li (Lead MLOps)
Summary (auto): Workshop to align on encryption at rest+in transit, KMS/BYOK/HSM integration options, audit logging and key rotation policies for Pioneer Medical Systems' regulated workloads (HIPAA scope). Action items captured for design artifacts and follow-ups.
Topics: encryption envelope patterns, BYOK vs Redwood-managed keys, HSM attestation, key rotation cadence, audit logs and log retention, data residency, RBAC/SSO interplay with key access, disaster recovery/escrow concerns.

Transcript:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hey everyone, thanks for carving time, um this is Lena from Redwood, and we'll kick off with a short agenda — quick compliance context, dive into key flow, options for BYOK/H-S-M onboarding, and wrap with next steps.
[00:18] Asha Gupta: Thanks Lena. From Pioneer side, main ask is we need to prove encryption controls for PHI processing, key custody where our compliance team keeps custody or at least has verifiable attestation. We are scoped for HIPAA and we do SOC2 Type II already.
[00:33] Tom Reynolds: Also latency sensitivity on some inference flows is a hard requirement. So any encryption approach that adds significant RTT to token inference is a concern.
[00:46] Diego Marquez: totally noted. We'll show envelope encryption patterns so the per-token path keeps keys out of path as much as possible. quick note, sometimes the transcript will say KV cash instead of KV cache, ignore that.
[01:03] Dr. Mei Li: one ask — our inferencing runs across multiple regions due to data residency. We have patient records that must not cross country boundaries, so keys and key policies have to reflect that.
[01:20] Rachel Chen: great, we'll call that out. high level questions: do you want Redwood to hold root keys and rotate on your behalf, or do you prefer BYOK with HSM attestation and split-escrow?
[01:31] Asha Gupta: we strongly prefer BYOK. Our legal and security teams insist on customer key custody for sensitive PHI keys; however we are open to Redwood holding ephemeral data keys, if master key stays with us.
[01:46] Lena Park: that's a common requirement. Redwood supports a BYOK flow: you can bring keys from your HSM or cloud KMS (we've done AWS KMS, GCP KMS, Azure Key Vault), and Redwood will use envelope encryption where customer-provided CMKs wrap data keys.
[01:59] Tom Reynolds: can you describe the handshake? Is it an import operation or remote-wrap? we want to avoid key material transit whenever possible.
[02:12] Diego Marquez: two primary patterns: 1) remote-wrap where your KMS performs the wrap operation — Redwood sends a plaintext data key generated locally to your KMS vault endpoint which immediately wraps it and returns ciphertext, or 2) you pre‑provision a key in your HSM and we perform an API-wrap call so raw root material never leaves your boundary. The second is preferred for strict custody.
[02:39] Asha Gupta: ok, remote-wrap is acceptable if the transport is authn+mtls, and we get attestations and audit trail. But for very sensitive datasets we want importless methods.
[02:53] Diego Marquez: yep — we support both. for importless we rely on KMS wrap APIs and HSM attestation. We'll also support an offline import if needed but that's heavier. note: some transcription tools miswrite BYOK as BYOB, haha.
[03:08] Rachel Chen: on attestation, we can request and archive Cloud KMS attestation tokens or HSM device certificates — helpful for audits. Redwood collects the attestation metadata into our audit logs which you can forward to your SIEM.
[03:23] Tom Reynolds: what about key rotation? our policy is 90 days for master key rotation and 30 days for data key rotation maybe. Is there automation?
[03:35] Diego Marquez: Yes. two layers: automated data-key churn inside Redwood's runtime (ephemeral data keys per model session) and scheduled rewrap or rotate operations for CMKs. For BYOK you control rotation schedule in your KMS; we can trigger rewraps and provide a compatibility window.
[03:52] Asha Gupta: rewraps are fine but we need to ensure existing persisted embeddings are re-encrypted or an index maintained. we can't lose ability to decrypt old tokens.
[04:05] Lena Park: understood — we have tooling for backward-compat re-encryption jobs and versioned key IDs attached to stored artifacts so you can map which CMK wrapped which blob.
[04:17] Dr. Mei Li: does Redwood store the unwrapped data key in memory for inference? that's a no-go for us.
[04:25] Diego Marquez: short answer: we never persist unwrapped CMKs. Data keys may be materialized in memory for the shortest time necessary in isolated runtime containers and wiped; we also use hardware-backed crypto on nodes and memory protections. for ultra-sensitive workflows you can require an HSM-protected wrap operation so plaintext data keys never transit Redwood.
[04:50] Asha Gupta: ok good, please capture that in the design doc, need language for legal.
[04:58] Lena Park: will do. next: audit logs — what level of logging and retention do you need?
[05:06] Asha Gupta: full key use logs for 12 months, with integrity checks. Also we need alerting on anomalous wrap/unwrapped attempts and any changes to key policy.
[05:19] Rachel Chen: Redwood's audit log supports per-operation records: wrap/unwrap, policy change, rotation events, plus client IP, principal, and request IDs. Retention and export are configurable — we can push to your SIEM via secure forwarding or to S3 in an encrypted bucket.
[05:34] Tom Reynolds: will those logs include the attestation chains from the HSM?
[05:39] Diego Marquez: yes we persist attestation metadata and certificate chains as part of the event payload so auditors can trace the device that wrapped the key.
[05:45] Dr. Mei Li: what about RBAC? we use SAML SSO and have fine-grained roles — devs, platform ops, compliance. Keys must only be usable by specific service principals.
[05:58] Rachel Chen: Redwood integrates with SAML/Okta and supports role-based key policies. You can map your groups to Redwood roles and then to key permissions: wrap/unwrap/list/manage. We also support per-API-key scoping so runtime tokens don't automatically get key unwrap rights unless explicitly granted.
[06:15] Asha Gupta: cool. Another concern: in disaster recovery, do we do key escrow? Our legal wants a sealed-escrow option where keys are split and held by two parties.
[06:27] Diego Marquez: split-key escrow is doable, we can support Shamir-split into multiple shares, store one share in your custody, one in Redwood's, or ship to a third party. For highest assurance you can require multi-party unwrap where two shares are combined in a controlled workflow.
[06:42] Lena Park: that can be documented as part of the DR playbook. The tricky part is operationally testing it without exposing keys — we recommend periodic controlled drills.
[06:53] Tom Reynolds: can you comment on FIPS and HSM certifications? We need KMS-backed HSMs to be FIPS 140-2 Level 3 for our PCI/HIPAA scope.
[07:05] Diego Marquez: Redwood can integrate with FIPS-certified HSMs via cloud KMS providers or on-prem HSMs — customers have used AWS CloudHSM, Azure Dedicated HSM, and specialized appliances. We collect device certs and can store them with audit events.
[07:19] Asha Gupta: For on-prem HSM we may require an air-gapped import process and a notarized key ceremony. Is that supported?
[07:30] Rachel Chen: yes, we have a manual import and notarized ceremony workflow — it's longer but it fits highly regulated customers. We'll provide checklist and sample paperwork.
[07:41] Dr. Mei Li: on performance: you mentioned envelope encryption — can you explain how that avoids per-inference KMS calls?
[07:50] Diego Marquez: Sure. We use a data-key caching and K-V cache strategy. Day-to-day inference uses ephemeral data keys cached in secure process memory and a server-side KV cache for model prefix tokens. The CMK is only used to unwrap/wrap data keys at creation/rotation events. So the hot path avoids blocking on remote KMS. There is still a cold path on first use.
[08:12] Tom Reynolds: what's the cache TTL and how do you prevent replay or key reuse across tenants?
[08:18] Diego Marquez: the cache TTL is configurable; defaults are short (a few minutes) for sensitive workloads. We partition caches per-tenant and include tenant ID and key-version in the cache key. Cache entries are authenticated and pinned to process identity.
[08:32] Lena Park: note: KV cash typo again, sorry.
[08:35] (laughter)
[08:38] Asha Gupta: acceptable. We also need to ensure the token-level telemetry that Redwood exposes doesn't leak PHI. How do you sanitize logs and traces?
[08:48] Rachel Chen: we support token scrubbing and PII redaction in logs. By default we don't log full request bodies for certain endpoints; you can opt-in for debug traces with explicit consent and timebound retention. We also mask embeddings in logs unless you allow storage for debugging.
[09:04] Tom Reynolds: data residency — we need keys and wrapped data to stay in the EU region for EU-sourced patient records. Is regional key binding supported?
[09:12] Diego Marquez: yes, we support region-bound CMKs. You can provision a CMK in a regional KMS and configure Redwood to route requests for that dataset only to the region-specific runtime. Policy-based routing plus model pinning help enforce that.
[09:29] Asha Gupta: ok, what happens if the primary region is down — do we fail open or fail closed? Our preference is fail closed for key access.
[09:38] Lena Park: Redwood can be configured to fail closed, which will reject requests requiring unwrap if the KMS endpoint is unreachable. There's also an optional degraded-mode where cached data keys can be used for a short window with strict auditing — but that is a policy decision you need to accept operationally.
[09:58] Dr. Mei Li: can Redwood's console show key usage breakdown per model and per-token cost associated with KMS unwraps? useful for our chargeback.
[10:07] Rachel Chen: yes, per-route and per-key telemetry. We expose a cost/latency breakdown including KMS calls so you can see financial impact of unwrap events.
[10:17] Tom Reynolds: legal follow-up: BYOK clauses — we need liabilities clarified around key compromise. Will Redwood sign a clause that says Redwood will not have access to your CMK plaintext and will provide attestations?
[10:29] Lena Park: we can provide contractual language and we've signed customer-facing BYOK addenda in previous deals. We'll route legal and security to align on the exact wording.
[10:36] Asha Gupta: great. A couple more specifics — do you do envelope encryption for embeddings store and does that affect similarity search latency?
[10:45] Diego Marquez: embeddings can be encrypted at rest; retrievals require decrypt. We support deterministic encryption modes for indexable fields and can perform server-side re-encryption during batch ingest to reduce per-query decrypts. For nearest neighbor search, we usually decrypt at the node level and keep plaintext only in memory for the query window; performance impact measured in past pilots was <8% for small clusters, but results depend on vector DB and sharding.
[11:14] Dr. Mei Li: any examples of customers in healthcare who've done BYOK with Redwood?
[11:20] Lena Park: we have references — we won't name PHI customers in the transcript, but we can provide anonymized case studies and an architecture whitepaper.
[11:29] Tom Reynolds: firewall/proxy requirements — what's the handshake to your control plane for key policy?
[11:35] Diego Marquez: API calls to the control plane are over mTLS with mutual client certs; we can do IP allowlisting and VPC peering. For private deploys, we can run control-plane components in your VPC so control calls never cross the public internet.
[11:53] Asha Gupta: for the pilot we probably want private deployment with our CMK in Azure Key Vault and a dedicated Redwood runtime in our VNet. What are network egress expectations?
[12:04] Rachel Chen: minimal egress: only to your KMS endpoints and Redwood control plane unless you enable outbound telemetry forwarding. We'll share a closed set of IP ranges and firewall rules in the onboarding doc.
[12:17] Tom Reynolds: about HSM lifecycle: key destruction and zeroization — how do you verify it's done downstream?
[12:25] Diego Marquez: HSM zeroization is usually certified by device logs and hardware attestation. For cloud HSMs, providers offer API-driven key deletion and rotation events. For on-prem HSMs we recommend a notarized destruction procedure with accompanying signed attestation. We'll archive those artifacts.
[12:44] Asha Gupta: we will want to see the code-level controls for key access inside Redwood runtime — e.g., process isolation, ephemeral containers, GRPC channel auth. Is there a developer-facing diagram you can share?
[12:57] Lena Park: yes Diego will produce an HSM integration and runtime diagram showing process boundaries, network ports, and token flows.
[13:05] Diego Marquez: i'll include PKCS#11 interactions, KMS wrap/unwrap flows, and where the attestation tokens are stored. Also note incompatibilities: some older HSMs don't support remote wrap APIs so that'll require a manual flow.
[13:19] Dr. Mei Li: monitoring — if we see an anomalous unwrap, how fast can we lock a CMK or revoke runtime permissions?
[13:28] Rachel Chen: you can configure automated policy triggers — on suspicious activity we can revoke runtime roles, rotate keys, or add deny-list entries. There is also a manual emergency suspend API that cuts unwrap privileges immediately across the fleet.
[13:43] Tom Reynolds: developer ergonomics: do you provide SDK hooks so our engineers can call Redwood with a wrapped data key or do you expect us to use Redwood's storage APIs?
[13:54] Diego Marquez: you have both options. SDK supports client-side wrap and sending wrapped blobs, or you can call Redwood storage APIs which will manage data keys and metadata. We'll document both patterns.
[14:06] Asha Gupta: final question — for attestation evidence for SOC2 and ISO auditors, will we get a packaged artifact with key event timeline, attestation certs, and role access lists?
[14:16] Rachel Chen: yes we can produce a compliance bundle that includes event timeline, signed attestations, key-version mappings, and RBAC snapshots for the requested period.
[14:26] Lena Park: ok let's recap and close with next steps.
[14:30] Lena Park: recap: Pioneer prefers BYOK with HSM attestation for PHI; Redwood supports both remote-wrap and importless wrap patterns; envelope encryption is the recommended hot-path; audit logs and attestation chains will be stored and exportable; region-bound CMKs and fail-closed behavior supported; action items: design diagram, network diagram, legal BYOK clause review, and SOC2/ISO docs.
[14:52] Asha Gupta: that matches our asks, thanks. Please include the notarized ceremony checklist for on‑prem HSM.
[14:59] Lena Park: will do. Any final words?
[15:03] Tom Reynolds: no, thanks all.
[15:05] Dr. Mei Li: thanks.

End of transcript.
